arguments.name: John Cook's thesis: Paul taught bodily resurrection
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas (reporting John Cook)
arguments.conclusion: Paul's view of the resurrection is that he saw the same bodily appearances of Jesus described in the Gospels (Matthew, Luke, John), not a ghostly or non-bodily view.
premises: John Cook states his thesis up front in his resurrection volume, published in the respected German Wissenschaftliche series.
Cook explicitly denies that Paul teaches a 'Casper' (ghostly) view of resurrection appearances.
Cook holds that Paul teaches the same bodily appearances found in Matthew, Luke, and John.

st1.quote: And he says in the beginning my thesis is that Paul's view of the resurrection is that he saw the same body as described in the Gospels, not Mark of course, but described in the Gospels on the resurrection appearances of Jesus.

st2.quote: He teaches the same bodily appearances Matthew, Luke, and John do.

st3.quote: they're both included in the uh German uh Wissenschaftliche series, which is now hundreds of volumes.

st4.quote: He teaches the same bodily appearances Matthew, Luke, and John do.

st5.quote: we said uh it would be nice, but we said this is inadequate for a whatever it was 600-700 page book on this topic.

st6.quote: He teaches the same bodily appearances Matthew, Luke, and John do.

st8.quote: So, does Michael Licona. So, does um uh Gundry in his book on Soma.

or1.quote: And he says in the beginning my thesis is that Paul's view of the resurrection is that he saw the same body as described in the Gospels
or1.why: Habermas is reporting Cook's own thesis rather than restating a prior argument of his own; it is a variant of the standard bodily-resurrection reading.

or2.quote: He's doing mostly Greco- Greco-Roman historiography.
or2.why: Points to Cook's Greco-Roman historiographical method as support, not standard in popular defenses.

or3.quote: He's doing mostly Greco- Greco-Roman historiography.

arguments.prior_art: John Cook, Resurrection in the Wissenschaftliche series (as reported by Habermas)
arguments.weakest_link: The inference from Cook's stated thesis to its truth: the source only reports what Cook says, not evidence that Paul actually taught this.
arguments.develop_next: Cite the specific Pauline texts (e.g. 1 Cor 15) Cook exegetes to show the thesis is textually grounded.

arguments.name: Bodily resurrection view is now widely accepted
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: The view that Paul believed in bodily resurrection is now very widely taught, despite being extremely unpopular when Cook's books first appeared.
premises: Cook's bodily-resurrection thesis was extremely unpopular when his volumes first came out.
The fact that Paul believes in bodily resurrection is now very widely taught by scholars today.

st1.quote: But now it's kind of taken the day, the fact that Paul believes in bodily resurrection is very widely taught today.

st2.quote: That's extremely impo- unpopular when this these books first came out or even after.

st4.quote: Very widely taught by the guys.

st6.quote: Very widely taught by the guys.

st8.quote: Now Dale Allison, just give you an example, Dale Allison said Paul believed in bodily resurrection appearance like the Gospels do.

or1.quote: But now it's kind of taken the day, the fact that Paul believes in bodily resurrection is very widely taught today.
or1.why: A sociological claim about scholarly consensus rather than a new argument.

or2.quote: That's extremely impo- unpopular when this these books first came out or even after.
or2.why: No new evidence beyond assertion of consensus.

arguments.weakest_link: The consensus claim is asserted without names, numbers or citations.
arguments.develop_next: Provide a survey or list of named scholars and works demonstrating the consensus.

arguments.name: Dale Allison concedes Paul meant bodily resurrection
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas (reporting Dale Allison)
arguments.conclusion: Even a scholar not personally committed to the bodily view, Dale Allison, affirms that Paul meant bodily resurrection.
premises: Dale Allison says Paul believed in bodily resurrection appearances like the Gospels do.
Allison states he is more open to non-bodily things and is not on the bodily side himself.
Allison insists one must distinguish what Paul said from what Bultmann said about Paul.

st1.quote: Dale Allison said Paul believed in bodily resurrection appearance like the Gospels do.

st2.quote: Dale says, "I'm more open to non-bodily things but I am telling you even though I'm not on that interpret- I'm not in the bodily side in my view, I think Paul meant bodily resurrection.

st3.quote: But, in volume three, he starts the book This might This might be the winner.

st4.quote: You have got to make this distinguish between what Paul said and somebody else going "Well, Bultmann says Paul believed bodily resurrection."

st5.quote: Dale says, "I'm more open to non-bodily things but I am telling you even though I'm not on that interpret- I'm not in the bodily side in my view, I think Paul meant bodily resurrection.

st6.quote: I think Paul meant bodily resurrection.

st8.quote: So, does Michael Licona. So, does um uh Gundry in his book on Soma.

or1.quote: Dale Allison said Paul believed in bodily resurrection appearance like the Gospels do.
or1.why: A citation of Allison's concession, a variant of the standard appeal to hostile-witness scholarship.

or2.quote: Dale says, "I'm more open to non-bodily things but I am telling you even though I'm not on that interpret- I'm not in the bodily side in my view, I think Paul meant bodily resurrection.
or2.why: Uses Allison's own non-commitment as evidence, a specific hostile-witness datum.

arguments.weakest_link: Relies on a paraphrased quotation without page citation from Allison's volume.

arguments.name: Bultmann affirmed Paul taught bodily resurrection
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: Bultmann himself acknowledged that Paul believed in bodily resurrection, even though Bultmann did not accept it.
premises: Bultmann can say Paul believed in bodily resurrection while personally rejecting it.
This is the distinction Allison was drawing between Paul's view and Bultmann's own view.

st1.quote: But But Bultmann can say Paul believed it, but I don't.

st2.quote: You have got to make this distinguish between what Paul said and somebody else going "Well, Bultmann says Paul believed bodily resurrection."

st4.quote: And that's what Dale was saying.

or1.quote: But But Bultmann can say Paul believed it, but I don't.
or1.why: A variant of the standard appeal to Bultmann's exegesis of Paul.

arguments.weakest_link: No textual citation is given for what Bultmann actually wrote about Paul.

Habermas and his interlocutor recognize the quote and attribute it to Wright.

or3.quote: that the resurrection is as knowable as the Rubicon?

arguments.name: Allison's Easter confession is a stunning testimony

premises: Allison writes: 'I believe that the disciples saw Jesus and that he saw them and next Easter will find me in church.'
Habermas finds this stunning after reading Allison for years.
Habermas ranks this comment as probably the best of the examples he could give.
